In the great epic **Mahabharata**, Krishna as an adult is adviser to the hero **Arjuna**. He drives his chariot. Before a great battle he explains to him how to act rightly. This conversation is called the **Bhagavad Gita** and is one of the most important scriptures of Hinduism.

On **Janmashtami** Hindus celebrate Krishna’s birthday. Many fast during the day and stay awake until **midnight**, because he is said to have been born at that time. People sing songs, decorate temples and act out scenes from his life. In Mathura the festival is celebrated especially grandly. Hindus in Switzerland also celebrate it in their temples.

gewusst: In a game on Janmashtami, young people form a human pyramid to reach a pot of butter or yoghurt hung up high.
The Hare Krishna movement has made the name Krishna known in Europe too.

teile.einleitung: A mandala is a picture, usually circular, with a clear centre. In Buddhism and Hinduism it represents a holy world and helps with meditation.
wichtigste: The Sanskrit word “mandala” means circle.
In Buddhism mandalas serve above all as an aid to meditation.
In the centre there is usually a Buddha or a deity.
Many Tibetan mandalas show a square with four gates inside a circle.
Tibetan monks scatter mandalas of coloured sand and then destroy them again.
The Swiss psychologist Carl Gustav Jung took an interest in mandalas.

abschnitte.text: **Mandala** is a word from **Sanskrit**, an ancient Indian language, and means “circle”. A mandala is a symmetrical picture arranged around a centre. The **centre** is the most important point. There a Buddha or a deity is usually shown, around whom everything else is ordered.

In many Tibetan mandalas you see inside the circle a **square with four gates**. It represents a palace. The gates face the **four points of the compass**. Whoever looks at the mandala is led by the eyes from the outside inwards to the centre. In this way you are meant to find inner calm. That is why the mandala serves above all as an aid to **meditation**.

Tibetan monks scatter special mandalas of **coloured sand**. With fine tubes they lay grain after grain for days into an artistic picture. When it is finished, it is **destroyed** again. The sand is swept together and often scattered in a river. This is meant to show that nothing in the world lasts for ever.

The Swiss psychologist **Carl Gustav Jung** from Küsnacht near Zurich painted mandalas himself. He saw in them a picture of the **wholeness of the soul**. He also had his patients paint mandalas. Today many children colour in mandalas at school, because it can be calming.

Some temples are built like a mandala. The best-known example is **Borobudur** on the island of Java in Indonesia. It was built around the year 800. Seen from above, the huge complex resembles a mandala made of stone. Pilgrims walk around it step by step up to the top.

gewusst: A sand mandala can take several days or even weeks of work and is swept away in the end all the same.
Borobudur is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: Mary was the mother of Jesus. She is especially honoured in Christianity, and in Islam too she has a place of honour under the name Maryam.
wichtigste: Mary lived about 2000 years ago in Galilee, in the area of present-day Israel.
She was engaged to Joseph and became the mother of Jesus.
The Bible tells how the angel Gabriel announced the birth of Jesus to her.
In the Catholic and Orthodox churches, Mary is especially honoured.
In the Quran she is called Maryam, and a whole sura is named after her.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Gospels**, Mary lived in **Nazareth** in Galilee. She was engaged to the carpenter **Joseph**. The angel **Gabriel** appeared to her and announced that she would be the mother of the Son of God. This event is called the **Annunciation**. According to tradition, Jesus was born in Bethlehem. The Bible also tells that Mary was present at the cross when Jesus died.

In the **Catholic** and **Orthodox** churches, Mary is especially honoured as the “Mother of God”. Many people pray the **Hail Mary**, a prayer that begins with the angel’s greeting. There are many feasts of Mary, for example the **Assumption of Mary** on 15 August. The Reformed churches respect Mary as a role model of faith, but do not venerate her in this way.

In the **Quran** too, Mary is greatly honoured. There she is called **Maryam**. A whole sura, that is, a chapter of the Quran, bears her name. She is the only woman mentioned by name in the Quran. For Muslims, Jesus, called Isa in Arabic, is an important prophet, but not the Son of God.

In Switzerland there are many churches and chapels dedicated to Mary. A well-known place of pilgrimage is **Einsiedeln** Abbey in the canton of Schwyz, with the **Black Madonna**. Many people make a pilgrimage there every year. The first name Maria and forms of it such as Marie or Mia are also very common.

gewusst: Mary is the only woman mentioned by her name in the Quran.
The Black Madonna of Einsiedeln is a wooden figure that turned dark over a long time from candle smoke.

teile.einleitung: You can often recognise Buddhist monks by their robes. Depending on the country, they are orange, dark red or black. The robe shows that a monk lives simply and gives up possessions.
wichtigste: In Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar many monks wear orange or saffron-yellow robes.
Tibetan monks mostly wear dark red robes.
Zen monks in Japan often wear black robes.
A monk’s robe in Thailand usually consists of three cloths.
In the past the robes were sewn from scraps of cloth.
Buddhist monks shave their heads.
A young monk who is still learning is called a novice.

abschnitte.text: The colour of the robe is not the same everywhere. In **Thailand**, **Sri Lanka** and **Myanmar** you see many monks in **orange** or saffron-yellow cloths. In **Tibet** the monks mostly wear **dark red** robes, often together with yellow cloths. Among the **Zen monks** in Japan the robes are often **black**. So the colour depends on the country and the tradition.

A monk in Thailand usually has **three parts**: an inner robe, an outer robe and a cloak. The cloths are not put on like a shirt, but **wrapped** around the body. In the past monks sewed their robes from old **scraps of cloth**. They were meant to live simply and own nothing expensive. To this day the pattern of many robes recalls pieces sewn together.

Buddhist monks **shave their heads**. This shows that appearance is not important to them. They own only a few things. In Thailand they go through the streets early in the morning with an **alms bowl**. People give them food. For the faithful this is a good deed, and the monks do not have to do their own shopping.

A young monk who is still learning is called a **novice**. In Thailand and Myanmar many boys become novices for a few weeks or months. In the monastery they learn the teaching of Buddha, pray and meditate. Afterwards many return to their usual life. Novices too wear a simple robe and have a shaved head.

gewusst: There are Buddhist monasteries in Switzerland too, for example a Thai monastery in Gretzenbach in the canton of Solothurn.
In the past the colour of the robes often came from plant dyes such as saffron or tree bark.

teile.einleitung: Many religions and cultures celebrate festivals of lights, especially in winter. When the days are short and dark, candles and lamps bring light and hope. Whether Hanukkah, Advent, Diwali or the Lucia festival: light stands for what is good.
wichtigste: In winter the days are short and dark, which is why festivals of lights are celebrated.
Jews celebrate Hanukkah, Christians Advent.
Diwali is the great festival of lights of the Hindus.
At Diwali small oil lamps are set out.
An Advent wreath usually has four candles.
In Sweden the Lucia festival is celebrated on 13 December.

abschnitte.text: In **winter** it gets dark early, and the nights are long. For a very long time people have lit fires, candles and lamps then. The light brings **warmth** and **hope** into the dark season. That is why many religions celebrate **festivals of lights** in winter. What they all have in common is that light is a sign of the good, which is stronger than the darkness.

The Jewish festival of lights **Hanukkah** lasts eight days. It recalls an **oil miracle** in the Temple in Jerusalem: according to tradition, the oil that should have lasted for one day lasted much longer. Each evening one more candle is lit. There is a special candelabrum for this, the **hanukkiah**. Children play with a spinning top and eat foods fried in oil.

In **Advent** Christians prepare for **Christmas**, the festival of the birth of **Jesus**. An **Advent wreath** usually has **four candles**, one for each Sunday of Advent. Every Sunday one more candle is lit. At Christmas many lights shine on the tree. They recall that for Christians Jesus is the light of the world.

**Diwali** is the great festival of lights of the **Hindus**. It is celebrated in autumn, usually in October or November. People set out many small clay **oil lamps** in and in front of their houses. They stand for the victory of light over darkness. People decorate their houses, wear new clothes and eat sweets.

In **Sweden** the **Lucia festival** is celebrated on **13 December**. A girl in a white dress wears a wreath of candles on her head. The festival recalls **Saint Lucia**. In Switzerland, children walk through the streets in November in the **Räbeliechtli procession** with hollowed-out, lit turnips and sing as they go.

gewusst: The name Lucia comes from the Latin word “lux”, which means light.
The candelabrum for Hanukkah has nine arms: eight for the days of the festival and one for the candle with which the others are lit.

teile.einleitung: The Pali Canon is the oldest completely preserved collection of Buddhist writings. It is written in the Pali language and is the sacred scripture of Theravada Buddhism.
wichtigste: The Pali Canon is also called the Tipitaka, which means “Three Baskets”.
The Vinaya Pitaka contains the rules of the order for monks and nuns.
The Sutta Pitaka contains Buddha’s discourses, including the Dhammapada.
The Abhidhamma Pitaka analyses the teaching systematically.
In the 1st century BC the canon was first written down in Sri Lanka.
Pali is one of the Middle Indo-Aryan languages.

abschnitte.text: The Pali Canon is divided into three collections. They are called **baskets**, in Pali **pitaka**. This is where the name **Tipitaka** comes from, in Sanskrit **Tripitaka**. Each basket contains a different kind of text. Together they form a very large collection.

The **Vinaya Pitaka** collects the rules for the life of monks and nuns and tells how these rules came about. The **Sutta Pitaka** contains the discourses of Buddha. It includes the well-known collection of verses, the **Dhammapada**, in the “Minor Collection”. The **Abhidhamma Pitaka** arranges the teaching in lists and examines the human mind. It is regarded as the youngest basket.

According to tradition, after Buddha’s death his disciples met at the **first council** in Rajagaha. There **Ananda**, Buddha’s companion of many years, recited the discourses. **Upali** recited the rules of the order. For a long time the texts were passed on only by word of mouth, and monks learned them by heart.

In the **1st century BC**, according to the chronicles of Sri Lanka, monks wrote down the canon for the first time. This happened in the monastery of **Aluvihara**, on **palm leaves**. The language **Pali** is a Middle Indo-Aryan language, related to the Prakrit languages. Today it is used mainly as a sacred language.

**Theravada**, which is widespread in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia, is based on the Pali Canon. Other branches of Buddhism use mainly Chinese and Tibetan collections of writings. Monks still recite texts from the Pali Canon in their prayers today.

gewusst: In Mandalay in Myanmar, the whole Pali Canon was carved into more than 700 marble slabs in the 19th century.
A “sutta” is a discourse, and the word corresponds to the Sanskrit word “sutra”.

teile.einleitung: The new year does not begin on 1 January everywhere. Different religions and cultures have their own calendars and their own New Year festivals. Some celebrate in autumn, others in spring.
wichtigste: The Jewish New Year is called Rosh Hashanah and falls in autumn.
On Rosh Hashanah people eat apple with honey and blow the shofar.
The Islamic calendar follows the moon and begins with Muhammad’s emigration in 622.
The Christian church year begins with the first Sunday of Advent.
Nowruz is celebrated around 21 March at the start of spring.
In Thailand people splash each other with water at Songkran in April.
New Year’s Eve is called Silvester in German, after Pope Sylvester I.

abschnitte.text: The Jewish New Year is called **Rosh Hashanah**, which means “head of the year”. It is celebrated in **autumn**, in September or early October. People dip **pieces of apple in honey** and wish each other a sweet new year. In the synagogue the **shofar**, a ram’s horn, is blown. Its loud note is meant to wake people up and make them think.

The **Islamic calendar** follows the **moon**. A lunar year is about 11 days shorter than a solar year. That is why the Islamic New Year falls about 11 days earlier every year. The calendar begins with the **Hijra**: in the year 622 the Prophet **Muhammad** emigrated with his followers **from Mecca to Medina**.

abschnitte.titel: Church year and New Year’s Eve
abschnitte.text: The Christian **church year** does not begin on 1 January, but with the **first Sunday of Advent**, four Sundays before Christmas. The civil year ends on 31 December, **Silvester** in German. The name comes from **Pope Sylvester I**, who died on 31 December 335. In Switzerland there are special customs at the turn of the year, for example **Silvesterklausen** in Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

**Nowruz** means “new day”. It is celebrated around **21 March**, when spring begins. Nowruz is especially important in **Iran**, but also in Afghanistan, among the Kurds and in Central Asia. In **Thailand** the New Year is called **Songkran** and falls in **April**. People cheerfully splash each other with water. Water stands for cleansing and good luck.

The **Chinese New Year** also follows a lunar calendar. It always falls on a day between 21 January and 20 February. Each year belongs to one of twelve **zodiac animals**, for example the dragon or the rabbit. People celebrate with family, fireworks and lucky red colours. It is the most important family festival in China.

gewusst: Nowruz has been on UNESCO’s list of intangible cultural heritage since 2009.
In Appenzell Ausserrhoden, New Year’s Eve is celebrated twice: on 31 December and, by the old calendar, on 13 January.

teile.einleitung: Orthodox Judaism is the branch of Judaism that holds especially strictly to the traditional commandments. Its followers live their everyday lives by Jewish religious law, the **Halakha**.
wichtigste: For Orthodox Jews, God gave the Torah to Moses on Mount Sinai.
The commandments of the Torah therefore apply to them unchanged.
On the Sabbath, Orthodox Jews do not drive and do not use electrical devices.
In Orthodox synagogues men and women sit separately.
Very strictly observant ultra-Orthodox Jews are called Haredim in Hebrew.
Orthodox Jews eat only food that is kosher according to the dietary laws.

abschnitte.text: At the centre is the **Torah**, the five books of Moses. For Orthodox Judaism, God gave it to Moses on Mount **Sinai**. This also includes the oral tradition, which was later written down in the **Talmud**. Because the commandments come from God, people may not simply change them. But rabbis interpret them for new questions, for example about modern technology.

The **Sabbath** begins on Friday evening and ends on Saturday evening. On this day of rest, many kinds of work are forbidden by religious law, including making a fire. That is why Orthodox Jews do not drive a car or switch on a light. Many walk to the synagogue. The day belongs to prayer, family and shared meals.

In Orthodox synagogues men and women sit in separate areas. There is often a **women’s gallery** or a partition called a **mechitza**. The service is held mainly in Hebrew. During prayer men wear a head covering, the **kippah**, and often a prayer shawl.

Orthodox Judaism is not uniform. The **Haredim**, which means “those who fear God”, live very strictly and often wear dark clothes. **Modern Orthodoxy** combines the commandments with a life in the middle of today’s society, with work and study. In Switzerland too, for example in Zurich and Basel, there are Orthodox communities.

The dietary laws are called **kashrut**. Permitted food is called **kosher**. Pork, for example, is forbidden. Meat and milk are not eaten together, and in Orthodox kitchens they are often even prepared with separate dishes.

gewusst: In some residential districts, Orthodox communities stretch a wire, the eruv. Within it, things may be carried on the Sabbath.
There are special Sabbath lifts that stop by themselves at every floor, so that nobody has to press a button.

teile.einleitung: The Easter fire is part of the Easter Vigil service in many Catholic churches. It is lit in front of the church and stands for Jesus Christ, who, according to Christian belief, rose from the dead.
wichtigste: The Easter fire burns on the night of Easter Vigil in front of many Catholic churches.
The priest blesses the fire.
The large Easter candle is lit from the Easter fire.
The light is then carried into the dark church.
The fire stands for the light that overcomes the darkness.

abschnitte.text: The **Easter Vigil** is the night before Easter Sunday. The service begins in the dark in front of the church. There the **Easter fire** burns, which the priest blesses. For Christians the fire shows that Jesus has defeated death, just as light drives away the night.

The large **Easter candle** is lit from the Easter fire. It bears a cross, the year and the Greek letters **alpha and omega**, the first and the last letter. The priest carries the candle into the dark church. People light their small candles from it, until the whole church is bright.

Outside the church too there are fires at Easter. In some areas, for example in northern Germany, large heaps of wood are lit, and many people gather around them. In many Catholic parishes in Switzerland, the fire in front of the church is a fixed part of the Easter Vigil.

gewusst: The Easter candle then burns all year at baptisms and at funeral services in the church.

teile.einleitung: Einsiedeln Abbey in the canton of Schwyz is one of the best-known monasteries in Switzerland. Benedictine monks live here, and many pilgrims come every year. Einsiedeln is the largest place of pilgrimage in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Einsiedeln lies in the canton of Schwyz.
The place is named after the hermit Meinrad, who lived here in the forest.
Two ravens can be seen in the coat of arms of the abbey and the village.
The abbey is led by an abbot, whom the monks elect.
Einsiedeln is the largest place of pilgrimage in Switzerland.
The abbey has a very old stud farm for horses.
A well-known pastry is the Einsiedeln ram.

abschnitte.text: More than 1,100 years ago the monk **Meinrad** withdrew into the dark forest. He lived there alone and prayed. A person who lives alone like this is called a **hermit**, in German “Einsiedler”. That is why the place later received the name **Einsiedeln**. Meinrad is revered today as a saint.

A legend tells that two **ravens** lived with Meinrad. After his death they are said to have pursued the culprits until they were caught. That is why the **coats of arms** of the abbey and the village show two ravens. You can still see them in many places in Einsiedeln.

In the 10th century a **Benedictine abbey** arose at Meinrad’s place. It is led by an **abbot**, whom the monks elect themselves. The large **abbey church** was built in the 18th century in the **Baroque** style and is splendidly decorated inside. In the Chapel of Grace stands the famous **Black Madonna**, a figure of Mary with a dark face.

abschnitte.titel: Pilgrims from all over the world
abschnitte.text: Einsiedeln is the largest **place of pilgrimage** in Switzerland. Every year very many **pilgrims** come to pray in the church. The place also lies on the **Way of St James**, which leads as far as Spain. Many pilgrims take home a **ram** as a souvenir, a gingerbread pastry in the shape of a ram.

For many hundreds of years the monks have bred **horses**. The stud farm is regarded as the oldest still existing stud farm in Europe. The abbey also has a **monastery school**, that is, a secondary school, and a large library. The monks work, pray and study according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

gewusst: The horses from Einsiedeln are also called “Cavalli della Madonna”, horses of the Mother of God.
Fahr Abbey on the Limmat also belongs to Einsiedeln Abbey.

teile.einleitung: Orphism was a religious movement in ancient Greece. It is named after the mythical singer Orpheus. The Orphics believed in an immortal soul that wanders through many lives.
wichtigste: Orphism is named after the singer Orpheus.
The sacred writings of the Orphics were attributed to him.
The formula “soma sema” means: the body is a tomb of the soul.
The Orphics believed in a cycle of rebirths.
Many gave up eating meat.
Gold leaves from graves give the dead advice for the underworld.
The Derveni Papyrus is regarded as the oldest surviving book in Europe.

abschnitte.text: In Greek legend **Orpheus** was a **singer** with a divine gift. With his music he is said to have moved even animals, trees and stones. He went down into the **underworld** to bring back his dead wife Eurydice. The **Orphics** saw him as their teacher. They attributed their sacred poems and writings to him.

The Orphics believed that the **soul is immortal**. According to their teaching, it wanders through several bodies. This is called a **cycle of rebirths**. The formula **“soma sema”** is well known: the body is a tomb of the soul. The philosopher **Plato** takes up this play on words in the dialogue “Cratylus”. Through a pure life the soul could free itself from the cycle.

The **Orphic life** involved fixed rules. Because the soul could also live in animals, many Orphics gave up **meat**. They therefore also avoided bloody **sacrifices**, which were otherwise usual in Greece. In this way they wanted to stay pure. Similar ideas are found among the followers of Pythagoras.

An important Orphic myth tells of the **child Dionysus**. The **Titans**, an old race of gods, killed him. **Zeus** punished them and burned them with his **lightning bolt**. According to the myth, humans arose from their **ashes**. That is why a human being carries both a Titanic and a divine inheritance. The divine part is the soul, which is to be set free.

In graves, thin, inscribed **gold leaves** were found. They give the dead advice for the underworld. They warn against the **spring of forgetfulness**. The dead person should instead drink from the spring of **Mnemosyne**, the goddess of memory. In 1962 the **Derveni Papyrus** was found in a grave near **Thessaloniki**. It contains a commentary on an Orphic poem about the origin of the gods and is regarded as the **oldest surviving book in Europe**.

gewusst: The Derveni Papyrus survived only because it was partly charred on a funeral pyre.
The myth of Orpheus inspired many operas, including one of the very first operas, “L’Orfeo” by Claudio Monteverdi.

teile.einleitung: In the belief of the Andean peoples of South America, Pachamama is Mother Earth. She gives good harvests and is still revered today by many people in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador and other countries.
wichtigste: Pachamama means Mother Earth.
The Quechua word “pacha” means world, earth and time all at once, and “mama” means mother.
August is regarded as the month of Pachamama.
Offerings are placed in a hole in the ground to “feed” the earth.
The maize drink chicha is a popular offering.
In 2008 Ecuador wrote the rights of nature into its constitution, and in 2010 Bolivia passed a law on the rights of Mother Earth.

abschnitte.text: For the **Quechua** and **Aymara** peoples the earth is alive. Pachamama gives people food, water and fertility for the fields. That is why one should thank her and not exploit her. The Aymara live mainly around **Lake Titicaca** in Bolivia and Peru.

Families dig a hole in the ground and fill it with food, drink and **coca leaves**. In this way, according to belief, the earth is “fed”. Before drinking, many people pour a few drops of **chicha** on the ground. Chicha is a drink made from maize. In this way Mother Earth gets the first sip.

In the Andes, **August** is the month of Pachamama. Then, according to belief, the earth is hungry and waits for gifts before sowing. During this time many communities hold special rituals. People often combine these old customs with Christian belief.

Alongside Pachamama, people revere the **Apus**. These are the spirits of the mountains, which according to belief live in the high peaks. They protect the people, animals and fields in their surroundings. Gifts are brought to them too.

The ideas around Pachamama have even shaped laws. In 2008 **Ecuador** became the first country to write the rights of nature into its constitution, and there it also calls her Pacha Mama. In 2010 **Bolivia** passed a law on the rights of Mother Earth. It describes the earth as a living system with rights of its own.

gewusst: Under the constitution of Ecuador, the rights of nature can be enforced in court.
The word “pacha” means space and time at once, that is, the whole world.

teile.einleitung: Mana is a word from languages of the Pacific islands. In the anthropology of religion it means an impersonal supernatural force that can work in people, things or places.
wichtigste: Mana comes from languages of Melanesia and Polynesia in the Pacific.
It means an impersonal, supernatural power.
The missionary Robert Henry Codrington made the term known in Europe in 1891.
Robert Ranulph Marett developed from it the theory of pre-animism.
Marcel Mauss and Henri Hubert saw in mana a key to magic.

abschnitte.text: On many islands in the Pacific, people believed in a special force called **mana**. It makes a person successful and powerful. A chief, a warrior or a special object can have a lot of mana. Mana is **impersonal**: it is not a god and not a spirit, but a kind of effective power.

The English missionary **Robert Henry Codrington** described mana in 1891 in his book “The Melanesians”. After that, scholars took over the term. They also used it for similar ideas in other cultures. In this way mana became a technical word of the **anthropology of religion**, the science of the religions of different peoples.

The scholar **Edward Tylor** thought that religion begins with belief in souls, **animism**. **Robert Ranulph Marett** disagreed: before that, he said, there had been a feeling for an impersonal power such as mana. This earlier stage he called **pre-animism**. The French scholars **Marcel Mauss** and **Henri Hubert** interpreted mana around 1903 as an idea that makes magical action seem effective. Today many researchers view such stage models critically.

gewusst: In many computer games the magic power of a character is called “mana”. The word originally comes from the Pacific.
The anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss called mana an “empty signifier”, that is, a word that can take on almost any meaning.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Egypt, Maat is both a goddess and an important idea. She stands for truth, justice and the right order of the world. Maat also played a large part in the judgement of the dead.
wichtigste: Maat stands for truth, justice and world order.
The goddess Maat wears an ostrich feather on her head.
At the judgement of the dead, the heart is weighed against the feather of Maat.
The composite creature Ammit devours the heart of a guilty dead person.
The opposite of Maat is called Isfet.
The pharaoh had to bring Maat about on earth.

abschnitte.text: **Maat** means the right **order** of the world, of society and of action. This includes **truth** and **justice**. The goddess Maat embodies this principle. She was regarded as the daughter of the sun god **Re**, who set up the world order at the creation. It was even said that Re lives on Maat.

The mark of the goddess is an **ostrich feather** on her head. The feather also serves as the **hieroglyph**, that is, the written sign, for her name. In pictures Maat is often seen as a seated woman with this feather. Sometimes she also has wings on her arms.

According to Egyptian belief, every dead person had to face a **judgement of the dead**. In it his **heart** was weighed on a scale against the **feather of Maat**. The heart was regarded as the seat of the **conscience**. If it was no heavier than the feather, the dead person was allowed to enter the **afterlife**. Otherwise **Ammit** devoured it, a composite creature of crocodile, lion and hippopotamus, and the dead person was destroyed for ever.

In the **Book of the Dead** there are spells for the way into the afterlife. In **Spell 125** the dead person declares before **42 judges of the dead** that he has not committed certain wrongs. He says, for example, that he has not stolen and not lied. This declaration is called the **negative confession**. In this way the dead person showed that he had lived according to Maat.

The opposite of Maat is called **Isfet**. It stands for **chaos**, injustice, lies and violence. The task of the **pharaoh** was to bring Maat about on earth and to drive out Isfet. The king was regarded as the guarantor of the world order. In rituals he presented the gods with a small **figure of Maat** as an offering.

gewusst: Many pictures of the judgement of the dead survive on papyrus scrolls that were laid in the grave with the dead.
The name Maat is found in royal names too: the female pharaoh Hatshepsut had the throne name Maatkare.

teile.einleitung: The Kumbh Mela is a great Hindu pilgrimage festival in India. Millions of people bathe in holy rivers during it. It is regarded as the largest religious gathering in the world.
wichtigste: At the Kumbh Mela pilgrims bathe in holy rivers to cleanse themselves of sins.
The festival takes place in turn in Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik.
“Kumbh” means pitcher.
In Prayagraj the Ganges, the Yamuna and the mythical Sarasvati meet.
Since 2017 the festival has been part of UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage.
The Naga Sadhus lead the procession to the royal bath.

abschnitte.text: The word **Kumbh** means **pitcher**, and Mela means festival or gathering. A myth tells of a pitcher with **amrita**, the nectar of immortality. Gods and demons fought over it. In the process, drops are said to have fallen to the earth in four places. It is exactly there that the Kumbh Mela is celebrated today.

The four festival sites are **Prayagraj**, **Haridwar**, **Ujjain** and **Nashik**. All lie on holy rivers. At each site the festival is celebrated about **every twelve years**. In Prayagraj the **Ganges** and the **Yamuna** visibly flow together. The **Sarasvati** is regarded as an invisible third river. This place is called **Triveni Sangam**.

The pilgrims step into the water to cleanse themselves of **sins**. Certain festival days are especially important. At the **Shahi Snan**, the royal bath, the **Naga Sadhus** enter the water first. These are ascetics, that is, people who give up almost everything. They are often covered in ash.

Place and time are calculated from the position of **Jupiter**, the **sun** and the **moon**. Above all, Jupiter is important, which takes about **twelve years** to orbit the sun. That is where the rhythm of the festival comes from. The very great **Maha Kumbh Mela** took place in Prayagraj in 2025.

The Maha Kumbh Mela of 2025 lasted from 13 January to 26 February. The government of Uttar Pradesh reported over **660 million** pilgrim visits. People who bathed several times were counted too. For the festival a huge **tent city** with roads, bridges and hospitals is built each time. In **2017** **UNESCO** added the Kumbh Mela to the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

gewusst: The huge crowds of the Kumbh Mela can even be seen from space on satellite images.
The tradition is passed on mainly by word of mouth and through taking part.

teile.einleitung: A dress code sets out what clothing is expected in a place. Such rules exist especially in churches, mosques and temples. They are a sign of respect for the place and for the people who pray there.
wichtigste: In many churches and temples you should cover your shoulders and knees.
Covered shoulders are seen as a sign of respect.
In mosques and Hindu temples you take off your shoes.
In a Sikh gurdwara everyone covers their head.
In Christian churches men traditionally take off their hats.
Schools, firms and parties can have dress codes too.

abschnitte.text: When visiting many **churches**, mosques and temples, you should cover your **shoulders**. Sleeveless clothes or very short shorts are often seen there as unsuitable. Covered shoulders and knees are a sign of **respect**. In large churches in Italy, people are sometimes reminded of this at the entrance. Sometimes you are even given a scarf to put around you.

The rules differ from religion to religion. In **mosques** and many **Hindu temples** you take off your shoes. In a mosque, women usually cover their hair. In a **gurdwara**, the house of worship of the Sikhs, everyone covers their head, men and women alike. In a **synagogue**, men wear a small head covering, the **kippah**. In Christian churches, by contrast, men traditionally take off their hats.

Dress codes exist not only in religions. Some schools have a **school uniform** or rules about clothing. In hospitals, in the police or in the kitchen, people wear **work clothes**, often for reasons of safety or cleanliness. For parties such as a wedding, the invitation sometimes says what clothing is wanted. If you are not sure, you can ask beforehand.

gewusst: In a Sikh gurdwara, visitors cover their heads too, often with a borrowed cloth.
In the synagogue men cover their heads, in church they take off their hats.

teile.einleitung: Mistletoe is a plant that does not grow in the ground, but high up on the branches of trees. The Celts already thought it sacred, and to this day it is part of customs around Christmas.
wichtigste: Mistletoe grows as a round bush on the branches of trees.
It has no roots in the ground and takes water and nutrient salts from the tree.
Mistletoe is evergreen.
Its berries are white, sticky and poisonous to humans.
Birds spread the seeds.
According to Pliny, the druids cut mistletoe with a golden sickle.
The mistle thrush is named after mistletoe.

abschnitte.text: **Mistletoe** grows as a round bush high up on the branches of broadleaved and coniferous trees. In winter, when the broadleaved trees are bare, you can see it especially well. Mistletoe has no roots in the ground. It taps into the tree and takes **water and nutrient salts** from it. But because it makes sugar itself with its green leaves, it is called a **hemiparasite**.

Mistletoe has **white, sticky berries**. They are **poisonous** to humans and must not be eaten. Birds like eating them, though. Afterwards they wipe the sticky **seeds** off on branches or pass them out. This allows a new mistletoe to grow on another tree. The **mistle thrush** is especially fond of mistletoe berries and is therefore named after it.

The **druids** were priests of the Celts. The Roman writer **Pliny** wrote that they cut mistletoe from the trees with a **golden sickle**. They considered a mistletoe growing on an oak especially sacred. Because mistletoe is **evergreen** and does not wither even in winter, it was once seen as a sign of life.

Especially in **England**, people hang up a sprig of mistletoe at Christmas. According to the custom, two people who meet under the sprig may give each other a **kiss**. In other countries too, people decorate their homes with sprigs of mistletoe during Advent. They are seen as bringers of good luck.

gewusst: In the “Asterix” comics, the druid Getafix cuts mistletoe with his golden sickle for the magic potion.
A mistletoe can live for many decades, as long as its branch does.

teile.einleitung: Martin Buber was a Jewish philosopher of religion. He was born in Vienna in 1878 and is best known for his philosophy of dialogue and the book “I and Thou”.
wichtigste: Buber was born in Vienna in 1878 and grew up in Lviv with his grandfather.
His main work “I and Thou” appeared in 1923.
Together with Franz Rosenzweig he began to translate the Hebrew Bible into German.
He collected Hasidic stories, for example “Tales of the Hasidim” from 1949.
In 1938 he emigrated to Jerusalem and taught at the Hebrew University.
In 1953 he received the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade.
He died in Jerusalem in 1965.

abschnitte.text: Martin Buber was born in **Vienna** in 1878. He then grew up with his grandfather in **Lviv**, which is in Ukraine today. There he got to know **Hasidism**, a devout Jewish movement with many stories and songs. Buber later collected its legends. In 1949 his collection **“Tales of the Hasidim”** appeared.

In 1923 Buber’s main work **“I and Thou”** appeared. In it he distinguishes two kinds of relationships. In the **I-Thou relationship** you meet someone completely and honestly. In the **I-It relationship** you treat something like an object that you use. For Buber, a person only becomes a person through meeting others. This school of thought is called **dialogical philosophy**.

In 1925 Buber began, together with **Franz Rosenzweig**, to translate the Hebrew Bible anew into German. They wanted to preserve the sound and rhythm of Hebrew as far as possible. The work is called **“Die Verdeutschung der Schrift”** (“The Germanisation of the Scripture”). After Rosenzweig’s death Buber carried on alone and only completed it in 1961.

Buber was active early on in the **Zionist movement**, which aimed at a Jewish state. In 1901 **Theodor Herzl** entrusted him with running the weekly newspaper **“Die Welt”**. From 1916 to 1928 Buber published the monthly journal **“Der Jude”**. He understood Zionism above all as a cultural and ethical renewal. For Palestine he wished for a **binational state** in which Jews and Arabs would live together with equal rights.

In 1938 Buber left Nazi Germany and went to **Jerusalem**. At the **Hebrew University** he taught social philosophy. In 1953 he received the **Peace Prize of the German Book Trade** in Frankfurt am Main. He accepted it as a sign of reconciliation, which was controversial in Israel. Buber died in Jerusalem in 1965.

gewusst: A well-known saying of Buber’s is: “All real living is meeting.”
Buber’s translation of the Bible took more than 35 years from start to finish.

teile.einleitung: The lotus position is a sitting posture with crossed legs. Many statues show Buddha in this posture. The lotus position is often used for meditating and in yoga.
wichtigste: In the lotus position you sit on the floor with crossed legs.
It is named after the lotus flower.
In the full lotus position the feet lie on the thighs.
It is often used for meditating.
The back is straight, and the hands often lie in the lap.
In many pictures Buddha sits on a lotus blossom.

abschnitte.titel: How you sit in the lotus position
abschnitte.text: In the **lotus position** you sit on the floor with **crossed legs**. In the **full lotus position** each foot lies on the other **thigh**, with the soles of the feet pointing upwards. This is not easy and needs a lot of practice. In the **half lotus position** only one foot is on top. In Sanskrit the posture is called **Padmasana**.

The lotus position is named after the **lotus flower**. The legs and feet look like the petals of an open blossom. The lotus flower grows in muddy water, but its blossom stays clean. In **Buddhism** this is a beautiful sign: a person too can become good and pure. In many pictures **Buddha** sits on a large lotus blossom as on a throne.

In the lotus position you sit calmly and steadily. That is why it is often used for **meditating**. The **back** should be **straight**, so that you can breathe calmly and well. Often the hands lie in the **lap**, one in the other, with the thumbs lightly touching. Many Buddha statues show exactly this posture.

The full lotus position is difficult for many people, especially for the **knees**. You should never force it. Whoever wants to meditate can also sit in the simple **cross-legged position** or on a cushion. You can also meditate well on a chair. What matters most is that you sit calmly and straight.

gewusst: The hand position in meditation has a name of its own, and such gestures are called mudras.
In yoga there are many postures named after animals or plants, such as the tree or the cobra.

teile.einleitung: Manichaeism was a religion founded in the 3rd century by Mani. It taught a struggle between light and darkness and spread from the Mediterranean as far as China.
wichtigste: Mani was born in 216 in the region of Babylonia in Mesopotamia.
In Manichaeism light and darkness stand opposed as first principles.
Mani saw Zarathustra, Buddha and Jesus as his predecessors.
He died around 276/277 in prison under the Great King Bahram I.
The community consisted of the Elect and the Hearers.
Augustine was a Manichaean Hearer for about nine years.
In the Uyghur Khaganate, Manichaeism was the state religion in the 8th century.

abschnitte.text: **Mani** was born in 216 in **Mesopotamia**, in the region of present-day Iraq. He proclaimed his teaching in the Persian **Sasanian Empire**. Mani saw himself as the last messenger in a line of prophets. As his predecessors he saw **Zarathustra**, **Buddha** and **Jesus**. That is why he took in elements from different religions.

Manichaeism teaches a strict **dualism**. This means that there are two opposed first forces: the good **light** and the evil **darkness**. According to this teaching, parts of the light are trapped in matter. Human beings are meant to help free this light.

The community was divided into two groups. The **Elect**, in Latin electi, lived very strictly and gave up a lot. The **Hearers**, in Latin auditores, lived less strictly. They supplied the Elect with food and everything necessary. The later Church Father **Augustine** belonged to the Hearers for about nine years. After turning to Christianity he wrote against the Manichaeans.

Under the Great King **Bahram I**, Zoroastrian priests gained influence at the Persian court. Mani was arrested and died around 276/277 in captivity. Later too, the Manichaeans were persecuted in many places, in the Persian Empire as well as in the Roman Empire.

All the same, the religion spread far to the east, along the **Silk Road**. The Uyghur ruler **Bögü Khagan** adopted Manichaeism in 762/763. The **Uyghur Khaganate** on the steppe is regarded as the only empire in which it was the state religion. Today there are no Manichaean communities any more.

gewusst: Nowadays, if someone is called “Manichaean”, it means that they divide the world strictly into good and evil.
Mani is also said to have been a gifted painter, and his followers decorated their books with splendid pictures.

teile.einleitung: Quetzalcoatl was one of the most important gods in Mesoamerica. His name means “Feathered Serpent”, and that is how he was shown: as a snake with colourful feathers.
wichtigste: Quetzalcoatl means “Feathered Serpent”.
The name comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.
Among the Maya the feathered serpent was called Kukulcán.
His great opponent was the god Tezcatlipoca.
According to one myth, he brought maize to humans.
As the wind god he was called Ehecatl.

abschnitte.text: The name joins the colourful **quetzal** bird with the word **coatl** for snake. It comes from **Nahuatl**, the language of the Aztecs. Nahuatl is still spoken today by more than a million people in Mexico. The quetzal with its long green tail feathers is the national bird of **Guatemala**, and the country’s currency is also called the quetzal.

For the **Aztecs**, Quetzalcoatl was a god of wisdom and a friend of humans. According to one myth, he turned himself into an **ant** and fetched the grains of maize out of a mountain. **Maize** was the most important food of the Aztecs. As the god of wind he was called **Ehecatl** and wore a mask with a beak. With his wind he announced the rain.

His great opponent was **Tezcatlipoca**, the “smoking mirror”. According to one legend, he drove Quetzalcoatl out of the city of **Tollan**. The two gods often stand for opposing forces. According to some legends, Quetzalcoatl promised to return one day.

The feathered serpent was worshipped long before the Aztecs. In **Teotihuacán**, one of the largest cities of ancient America near Mexico City, stands the **Temple of the Feathered Serpent**. It is decorated with stone serpent heads. The **Maya** called the god **Kukulcán**. The great pyramid of **Chichén Itzá** is dedicated to him.

In the year 1519 the Spaniard **Hernán Cortés** came to Mexico. A well-known legend says that the Aztec ruler **Moctezuma** took him for the returned Quetzalcoatl. Many historians today regard this story as a later invention, however. All that is certain is that it was told for a long time.

gewusst: The quetzal bird lives in mountain forests and can hardly be kept in captivity.
A giant species of pterosaur from the Cretaceous period was named Quetzalcoatlus after the god.

teile.einleitung: Neopaganism, or neo-heathenism, is the name given to religious movements that take up old pre-Christian religions. They arose above all in the 20th century. Many groups worship nature gods and celebrate the seasons.
wichtigste: “Paganus” is Latin and was later used for people who were not Christian.
Neopagan groups refer to Celtic, Germanic, Baltic or other ancient religions.
Many celebrate festivals through the year, for example at the solstice.
The researcher Margaret Murray influenced the movement with a theory that has since been disproved.
In 1964 Ross Nichols founded the Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids.
Romuva takes up the old religion of Lithuania.

abschnitte.text: The word **heathen** used to mean people who did not believe in the Christian God. **Neopagans** deliberately take up old, pre-Christian religions. These include Celtic, Germanic, Baltic, Slavic or Greek traditions. Often little is known about these old religions. That is why today’s customs are mostly **newly shaped**. Many groups worship several gods and regard **nature** as sacred.

The British researcher **Margaret Murray** wrote the book “The Witch-Cult in Western Europe” in 1921. She claimed that a pre-Christian **witch cult** had survived in Europe and that the witch trials had persecuted it. This theory is regarded today as **disproved**. Even so, it strongly influenced neopaganism. The movement **Wicca**, which arose in England, was later built on such ideas.

The ancient **druids** were priests and scholars of the Celts. Since the 18th century there have been druid orders again in Great Britain. **Ross Nichols** founded the **Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids** in **1964**. The order arose after a dispute in an older druid group. Today it is one of the best-known organisations of modern druidry. Celebrations at the **solstice**, for example at Stonehenge, are well known.

**Lithuania** was the last country in Europe to be Christianised, only around the year 1400. The neopagan movement **Romuva** takes up this old Baltic religion. It worships gods such as the thunder god **Perkūnas**. **Fire rituals** and old **folk songs** are important. In Scandinavia and Iceland there is a similar movement that appeals to the Germanic gods. It is called **Ásatrú**.

gewusst: In Iceland the Ásatrú community has been a state-recognised religious community since 1973.
Many neopagan groups celebrate eight festivals in the year, including the summer and winter solstices.

teile.einleitung: Mahayana is one of the great branches of Buddhism. The name means “great vehicle”, because this teaching wants to carry as many beings as possible to liberation.
wichtigste: Mahayana means “great vehicle” in Sanskrit.
At the centre stands the bodhisattva, a being who out of compassion wants to help everyone.
Mahayana is found mainly in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam.
Avalokiteshvara is the bodhisattva of compassion, called Guanyin in China.
The Heart Sutra contains the famous saying “Form is emptiness”.
A central concept is shunyata, emptiness.

abschnitte.text: In Buddhism the teaching is compared to a **vehicle** that carries people across the river of suffering. **Mahayana** calls itself the “great vehicle” because it wants to liberate not only the individual but all beings. It arose in India at about the turn of the era. Along the **Silk Road** it reached China and from there Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

A **bodhisattva** is a being who strives for enlightenment. Out of **compassion**, however, it gives up entering fully into nirvana until all beings are liberated. The best known is **Avalokiteshvara**, the bodhisattva of compassion. In China he is worshipped as **Guanyin**, in Japan as **Kannon**.

An important concept is **shunyata**, emptiness. This does not mean that nothing exists. It means that nothing has a fixed, independent nature, because everything depends on something else. The short **Heart Sutra** sums this up in the saying “Form is emptiness”. In East Asia this text is often recited together, that is, spoken or sung aloud.

In Mahayana there is not only the historical Buddha. In **Pure Land Buddhism**, **Amitabha** stands at the centre. Believers call on his name in order to be reborn in the “Pure Land” of the West. **Maitreya** is regarded as the Buddha who will appear in the distant future. In China he is often shown as a laughing, fat monk.

gewusst: The laughing, fat Buddha that you often see in Chinese restaurants is usually a picture of Maitreya.
Zen Buddhism from Japan also belongs to Mahayana.

teile.einleitung: Puja is the word for the worship of the gods in Hinduism. At a puja people pray, sing and bring the gods small offerings.
wichtigste: A puja is a worship of the gods.
It takes place at home or in the temple.
People bring flowers, fruit or sweets as an offering.
Incense sticks are often burning.
At the aarti, a small lamp is waved in front of the image of the god.
The blessed food is called prasad and is shared.

abschnitte.titel: At home and in the temple
abschnitte.text: Many Hindus have a small **altar** at home with pictures or figures of the gods. There they hold a short **puja** every day. Larger pujas take place in the **temple**. Before entering a Hindu temple, people take off their **shoes** so that the holy place stays clean. In Switzerland too there are Hindu temples, many of them founded by Tamils from Sri Lanka.

At a puja people give the gods **flowers**, **fruit** or **sweets**. This is a sign of thanks and love. **Incense sticks** are often burning, which smell sweet and whose smoke rises upwards. At the start a small **bell** is rung. It is meant to attract the attention of the gods.

A beautiful part of the puja is the **aarti**. A small lamp with a flame is waved in a circle in front of the image of the god. The people sing a song as they do so. Afterwards many briefly hold their hands over the flame and bring them to their eyes and forehead.

The food that was offered to the gods is regarded afterwards as blessed. It is called **prasad**. It is handed out to everyone and eaten together. In this way everyone receives a share of the blessing.

gewusst: At big festivals such as Diwali, families hold especially beautiful pujas with many lights.
The word “puja” comes from Sanskrit, the ancient language of India.

teile.einleitung: Mahatma Gandhi was an Indian lawyer and freedom fighter. With non-violent resistance he led India to independence from Britain and became a role model for peaceful protest all over the world.
wichtigste: Gandhi was born in 1869 in Porbandar in India and was actually called Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi.
“Mahatma” is an honorary title and means “great soul”.
He called his method of non-violent resistance Satyagraha, “holding on to truth”.
With the Salt March of 1930 he protested against the British salt tax.
The spinning wheel became his sign of self-reliance.
India became independent in 1947.
On 30 January 1948 Gandhi was shot in Delhi by the Hindu nationalist Nathuram Godse.

abschnitte.text: Gandhi studied law in London and afterwards worked for many years as a lawyer in **South Africa**. There Indians were disadvantaged by laws. Gandhi fought against this, but without violence. This is how his method **Satyagraha** arose. Whoever uses it openly breaks unjust laws and accepts the punishment, without hating the opponent.

The British government had a **salt monopoly**: only it was allowed to make and sell salt, and a tax was levied on it. In 1930 Gandhi walked with followers about 385 kilometres to the sea at **Dandi**. There he made salt himself from sea water. Thousands of people followed his example. The march made the independence movement known all over the world.

Gandhi wanted India to become economically independent. This idea was called **Swadeshi**. He called on people to spin and weave their own cloth instead of buying British textiles. He himself sat at the **spinning wheel**, called charkha in Hindi, every day. It became the sign of the whole movement.

In 1909, on a sea voyage from London to South Africa, Gandhi wrote the book **“Hind Swaraj”**. In it he criticises modern civilisation and demands that India govern itself. In the 1920s he wrote his autobiography **“The Story of My Experiments with Truth”**. He wrote both works in his mother tongue, **Gujarati**.

At independence in 1947 the country was divided into India and **Pakistan**. Serious unrest broke out. Gandhi worked for peace between Hindus and Muslims. The Hindu nationalist **Nathuram Godse** reproached him for going too far to meet the Muslims, and shot him in 1948 on his way to prayer. Gandhi’s ideas later influenced people such as **Martin Luther King** and Nelson Mandela.

gewusst: Gandhi’s birthday, 2 October, is now the United Nations’ International Day of Non-Violence.
Although Gandhi was nominated several times, he never received the Nobel Peace Prize.
In India Gandhi is often lovingly called “Bapu”, which means “father”.

teile.einleitung: Laïcité means that state and religion are clearly separated from each other. The state favours no religion and does not interfere in questions of faith. This principle is especially well known in France, but the canton of Geneva also has a long tradition of laïcité.
wichtigste: Laïcité means the separation of state and religion.
In France the law on the separation of church and state of 9 December 1905 applies.
Article 1 of the French constitution calls France a secular republic.
Alsace-Moselle is exempt from the separation law to this day.
Geneva adopted a laïcité law in 2019.
In 1980 Swiss voters rejected the complete separation of church and state.

abschnitte.text: The word **laïcité** comes from the Greek word for “people”, as opposed to the clergy. A **secular state** favours no religion and funds no religious community. At the same time it protects **freedom of conscience**: everyone may believe what they like, or nothing at all. Supporters see in this equal treatment, while critics sometimes worry about the visibility of religion in everyday life.

In **1881/82** the education minister **Jules Ferry** introduced free, compulsory and secular **primary schooling**. Religious instruction was removed from the curriculum of state schools. On **9 December 1905** came the law on the **separation of church and state**. Since then the state has recognised and funded no religious community. **Article 1** of the constitution of 1958 begins: “La France est une République indivisible, laïque, démocratique et sociale.”

One area is exempt to this day: **Alsace-Moselle**. In 1905 it belonged to the German Empire. After its return to France in 1919, the **Concordat of 1801** remained in force there, and the state still pays clergy. A law of **2004** forbids **conspicuous religious symbols** in public schools. Discreet symbols remain allowed.

In the canton of **Geneva**, church and state were already separated in **1907**. In **2019** the voters of Geneva adopted a new **laïcité law**. Those who represent the state should appear religiously neutral in office and wear no visible religious symbols. At federal level, on **2 March 1980** the voters rejected a popular initiative for complete separation, with about **79 per cent** No. That is why in Switzerland the **cantons** still regulate the relationship with the churches.

gewusst: In Alsace there are therefore two extra public holidays to this day, Good Friday and 26 December.
In Switzerland the situation differs from canton to canton: some levy church taxes, while Geneva is secular.

teile.einleitung: Maimonides was one of the most important Jewish scholars of the Middle Ages. He was a rabbi, philosopher and physician, and lived in the 12th century in Spain, North Africa and Egypt.
wichtigste: Maimonides was actually called Moses ben Maimon and was born in Córdoba in 1135 or 1138.
He is also known by the abbreviation “Rambam”.
His law code, the Mishneh Torah, is divided into 14 books.
He wrote his main philosophical work, “The Guide for the Perplexed”, in Arabic.
He formulated 13 principles of faith.
In Egypt he was a physician at court.
He died in 1204, and according to tradition his grave lies in Tiberias.

abschnitte.text: Moses ben Maimon was born in **Córdoba** in Spain, which was under Muslim rule. When the **Almohads** came to power, Jews and Christians were persecuted. The family fled to Morocco and later to **Egypt**. There Maimonides lived in Fustat near Cairo, where he died in 1204. According to tradition, his remains were taken to **Tiberias** on the Sea of Galilee.

The **Mishneh Torah** is a great law code in Hebrew. In it Maimonides arranged the whole of Jewish religious law clearly in **14 books**. This way rules could be found faster, without having to search the whole Talmud. The work is still studied today.

His main philosophical work is called **“The Guide for the Perplexed”**. He wrote it in **Arabic**, but with Hebrew letters. Maimonides wanted to join the Jewish faith with the teaching of the Greek philosopher **Aristotle**. He knew him through Arabic thinkers such as Avicenna and Averroes. He was convinced that reason and revelation do not contradict each other.

In his commentary on the Mishnah, Maimonides set out **13 principles of faith**. These include the unity of God and belief in the Messiah. Later they were taken into worship as the hymn **“Yigdal”**. Maimonides is also known as **Rambam**, an abbreviation for “Rabbi Moses ben Maimon”.

Besides his work as a scholar, Maimonides was a **physician**. In Cairo he served as personal physician at the court of the **Ayyubids** at the time of Sultan Saladin. He also wrote medical treatises, for example on healthy diet and way of life.

gewusst: A Jewish saying goes: “From Moses to Moses there was none like Moses”, meaning Maimonides.
The similar abbreviation “Ramban” refers to a different scholar, namely Nahmanides.

teile.einleitung: Liberal Judaism is a movement in Judaism that wants to adapt the religion to modern times. It arose in the 19th century in Germany. Here women and men have the same religious rights.
wichtigste: Liberal Judaism arose in the 19th century in Germany.
An important reformer was Abraham Geiger.
Women can become rabbis.
In 1935 Regina Jonas was ordained as the first woman rabbi in the world.
In Zurich the liberal Jewish community is called Or Chadasch.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many Jews in Germany wanted to adapt their religious life to **modern times**. Reformers such as **Abraham Geiger** worked for this. Sermons were given in **German**, and in some synagogues an organ was played. The movement later spread especially in the **USA**. There it is often called **Reform Judaism**.

In Liberal Judaism **women and men** have the same religious rights. They sit together at worship. Women can read from the Torah and become **rabbis**. In Orthodox communities this is not allowed. The religious commandments are regarded as important, but each person should examine for themselves how they live them in everyday life.

**Regina Jonas** from Berlin was ordained in **1935** as the first woman rabbi in the world. Ordained means that she was solemnly installed in her office. This was done by Rabbi **Max Dienemann** in Offenbach am Main. During the time of National Socialism she was persecuted. In **1944** she was murdered in **Auschwitz**.

There are liberal Jewish communities in Switzerland too. In **Zurich** this is the **Liberal Jewish Community Or Chadasch**. The name means **“new light”**. It is one of the largest liberal Jewish communities in Switzerland. Alongside it there are also Orthodox and other Jewish communities in Switzerland.

gewusst: In Liberal Judaism girls too often celebrate a big festival for religious maturity, the bat mitzvah.
The memory of Regina Jonas was long forgotten and became known again only after 1990.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Rome the Lares were protective gods of the house and the family. Every Roman family worshipped them at a small household altar. Together with other household gods they belonged to the everyday religion of the Romans.
wichtigste: The Lares protected the house and the family.
Their small household altar was called a lararium.
The Penates watched over the stores.
The Genius was the guardian spirit of the head of the family.
The Lares were given food, wine and incense as offerings.
In Pompeii many lararia are well preserved.

abschnitte.text: The **Lares** watched over the house and all who lived in it. These included the family, but also servants and slaves. The Romans believed that the Lares brought luck and protection. Alongside them were the **Penates**, who watched over the **pantry**. Lares and Penates were often worshipped together.

The small household altar for the Lares was called a **lararium**. It was a niche in the wall or a small shrine, often in the kitchen or the entrance area. There stood small **figures** of the household gods, or they were painted on the wall. Often you also see the **Genius**, the guardian spirit of the master of the house. He was usually shown as a man with an offering bowl.

At meals and festivals the Lares received small **offerings**. These included **food**, **wine**, flowers and **incense**. At important events in the family the Lares were honoured in a special way. In this way the household gods were firmly part of everyday life. In pictures the Lares are usually two **dancing young men** in short tunics, with a drinking horn and a bowl.

Not only houses had Lares. The **Lares Compitales** protected the **crossroads** of the neighbourhood. There stood small shrines. In their honour people celebrated the festival of the **Compitalia**. All the residents of a district took part.

In **79 AD** **Vesuvius** erupted and buried the city of **Pompeii** under ash. As a result many painted **lararia** were preserved. Today they can be seen at the excavations. They show how important the household gods were to the Romans. In Switzerland too, small bronze figures of gods have been found in Roman settlements such as **Augusta Raurica**.

gewusst: The word “Lar” can still be found in some languages today: in Portuguese “lar” means home.
Many household gods were shown on small statuettes that were hardly bigger than a hand.

teile.einleitung: The Oracle of Delphi was the most famous place of prophecy in ancient Greece. People from the whole Greek world travelled there to ask the god Apollo for advice. His answers were announced by a priestess, the Pythia.
wichtigste: Delphi lies on the southern slope of Mount Parnassus in central Greece.
The priestess who announced the prophecies was called the Pythia.
At the temple of Apollo stood the saying “Know thyself”.
The stone called the omphalos was regarded as the navel of the world.
According to myth, Apollo killed the serpent Python there.
King Croesus misunderstood an oracle.
Every four years the Pythian Games took place.

abschnitte.text: **Delphi** lies on the southern slope of **Mount Parnassus** in central Greece. Parnassus was also regarded as the seat of the **Muses**, the goddesses of the arts. According to myth, the dragon-like serpent **Python** guarded the place. The god **Apollo** killed it and founded his **sanctuary** here. Today the ruins of Delphi are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

According to the legend, **Zeus** let two eagles fly towards each other from the ends of the world. They met above Delphi. That is why Delphi was regarded as the **centre of the world**. A special stone, the **omphalos**, marked this spot. Omphalos means “navel”. A copy of the stone can be seen today in the museum of Delphi.

The prophecies were spoken by a priestess, the **Pythia**. She sat on a **tripod** in the temple and passed on the answers of the god. **Priests** interpreted her words and delivered them. Many answers were **ambiguous**. Above the entrance of the temple stood the saying **“Know thyself”**, in Greek “Gnothi seauton”. It warned people to know their limits.

A famous example is **Croesus**, the rich king of **Lydia**. He asked the oracle whether he should wage war against the Persians. The answer was that he would **destroy a great empire** if he crossed the river **Halys**. Croesus set off and lost. The great empire that he destroyed was his **own**.

Every four years the **Pythian Games** took place in Delphi. They honoured Apollo. After the Olympic Games they were the most important contests in Greece. Besides sport there were important **music competitions**, because Apollo was also the god of music. The winners received a **laurel wreath**.

gewusst: The name Croesus is still used today for a very rich person.
The city of Athens built its own small treasury in Delphi for its votive gifts.

teile.einleitung: The Qingming Festival is a Chinese day of remembrance for the dead ancestors. In spring, families visit the graves of their ancestors, clean them and bring offerings.
wichtigste: In German the festival is often called the festival of remembrance of the dead or the grave-sweeping festival.
It usually takes place on 4 or 5 April.
Qingming means “clear and bright”.
Families clean the graves and bring food, flowers and incense sticks.
Traditionally people also fly kites.
Since 2008 the festival has again been an official public holiday in the People’s Republic of China.

abschnitte.text: The name **Qingming** means “clear and bright” and describes the spring weather. It is also the name of one of the **24 periods** of the Chinese solar year. Because the festival follows the sun, it usually falls on **4 or 5 April**, rarely on 6 April. This makes it one of the few Chinese festivals with an almost fixed date.

At the Qingming Festival, families visit the **graves of their ancestors**. They pull up weeds, sweep the grave and bring **food**, **flowers** and **incense sticks**. Some also burn paper money as an offering for the dead. In this way people show respect to their ancestors. Honouring ancestors has been important in China for a very long time.
Because the festival is in spring, many families also go on **outings** into the countryside. Traditionally they fly **kites**. So the festival combines sorrow and remembrance with joy at the spring.

Closely linked with Qingming is the older **Hanshi Festival**, the Cold Food Festival. On this day, traditionally, no fire could be lit, so people ate cold food. It fell shortly before Qingming and later merged with it.

Since **2008** the Qingming Festival has again been a legal holiday in the People’s Republic of China. Many people then travel to their home towns. The day is also important in **Taiwan**, **Hong Kong** and Macau, and among many Chinese people abroad. In Taiwan and Hong Kong it is also a public holiday.

gewusst: At Qingming, in some areas people eat green dumplings made of rice flour, coloured with herbs.
Because so many people travel to the graves, trains and roads in China are especially crowded on these days.

teile.einleitung: Michael is a first name that comes from Hebrew. It means “Who is like God?” and is also the name of an archangel in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
wichtigste: Michael is a Hebrew first name.
It means “Who is like God?”.
The question is meant like this: no one is like God.
Michael is the name of an archangel.
The name is common in many languages, for example as Michel, Mikael or Miguel.

abschnitte.text: The name **Michael** comes from **Hebrew**. It is made up of the parts “mi” (who), “ka” (like) and “El” (God). Together that means: “**Who is like God?**” The question is not meant seriously, as the answer is already in it: no one is like God. So the name expresses reverence for God.

**Michael** is the name of an **archangel**, that is, an especially important angel. He appears in the Bible, for example in the Book of Daniel and in the Book of Revelation. There he fights a dragon that stands for evil. That is why he is often shown with a sword and armour. In Islam too Michael is known as an angel, where he is called **Mikail**. His feast day in the Catholic Church is **29 September**.

Because the archangel is honoured in many countries, the name is widespread. In French he is called **Michel**, in Swedish **Mikael**, in Spanish **Miguel**, in Italian **Michele** and in Russian **Mikhail**. Female forms are, for example, **Michaela** and Michelle. In Switzerland too, Michael has been a common first name for decades.

gewusst: Mont-Saint-Michel in France is a famous abbey island named after the archangel Michael.
Many churches in Switzerland are called St Michael’s Church.

teile.einleitung: Ludwig Feuerbach was a German philosopher of the 19th century. He became famous for his criticism of religion. He thought that human beings had imagined God in their own image.
wichtigste: Ludwig Feuerbach lived from 1804 to 1872.
In 1841 his main work “The Essence of Christianity” appeared.
According to his projection theory, human beings transfer their own nature to God.
His saying is: “Theology is anthropology.”
He belonged to the Young Hegelians.
The saying “You are what you eat” comes from him.

abschnitte.text: **Ludwig Feuerbach** was born in Bavaria in 1804 and died in 1872. He first studied theology and then philosophy under **Hegel** in Berlin. Later he turned against Hegel’s **idealism**, that is, the idea that spirit is the most important thing. With thinkers such as **Bruno Bauer** and **David Friedrich Strauss** he counts among the **Young Hegelians**. This group developed Hegel’s teaching further in a critical way.

In **1841** his main work **“The Essence of Christianity”** appeared. In it he interpreted religion as an expression of human qualities. Human beings, he said, imagine their best qualities such as **love**, **wisdom** and **goodness** as an infinite being outside themselves. This being they call God. This is called the **projection theory**: human beings transfer, or “project”, their nature onto God. Believers see this quite differently and hold God to be real.

Feuerbach summed up his criticism in one sentence: **“Theology is anthropology.”** Theology is the study of God, and **anthropology** the study of human beings. Whoever speaks about God, according to Feuerbach, is really speaking about human beings. His saying **“You are what you eat”** of 1850 is well known too. It expresses that thinking also depends on the body.

In **1848/49** Feuerbach gave lectures on the essence of religion in **Heidelberg**. Among the listeners was the Swiss poet **Gottfried Keller** from Zurich. Afterwards Keller turned away from belief in God and immortality. Feuerbach’s thinking also shaped his novel **“Green Henry”**.

**Karl Marx** too was influenced by Feuerbach. In **1845**, however, he wrote eleven short **“Theses on Feuerbach”**. In them he reproached him for looking at human beings only in the abstract. The famous eleventh thesis demands that the world should not only be **interpreted**, but **changed**.

gewusst: Feuerbach wrote the saying “You are what you eat” in a book review about the physiologist Jakob Moleschott, who later taught in Zurich.
For many years Feuerbach lived withdrawn in a small village in Franconia.

teile.einleitung: The Western Wall in Jerusalem, in German called the “Wailing Wall”, is the most important place of prayer in Judaism. It is a remnant of the wall that once supported the Temple Mount. Every day many people pray there and push slips of paper with wishes between the stones.
wichtigste: The Western Wall stands in the old town of Jerusalem.
It is part of the western retaining wall of the Temple Mount, which Herod had built.
In Hebrew it is called Kotel, “wall”, often also the Western Wall.
Its German name, “Wailing Wall”, comes from mourning for the destroyed Temple.
Visitors push slips of paper with prayers into the cracks.
On the Temple Mount today stands the Dome of the Rock with its golden dome.

abschnitte.titel: A remnant of the old wall
abschnitte.text: The **Western Wall** is part of the western **retaining wall** that King **Herod** had built around the Temple Mount. The Jewish **Temple** once stood on this platform. In the year 70 AD the Romans destroyed the Temple. The wall remained standing. In Hebrew it is called **Kotel**, which means “wall”. People often also say **Western Wall**, because it lies on the western side of the Temple Mount.

For centuries Jews have prayed at this wall and mourned the destruction of the Temple. That is why Europeans called it the **Wailing Wall**. Today it is the most important **place of prayer** in Judaism. At the wall, men and women pray in separate areas. Many celebrations take place here too, such as the bar mitzvah of boys.

abschnitte.titel: Slips of paper in the cracks
abschnitte.text: Many visitors write **prayers and wishes** on small slips of paper. These they push into the cracks between the large stones. Because so many slips collect, they are gathered up regularly. They are not thrown away but buried on the **Mount of Olives**. People of other religions visit the wall too.

On the Temple Mount today stand two important buildings of Islam. The **Dome of the Rock** with its **golden dome** was built at the end of the 7th century. It stands roughly where the Temple once stood. Next to it lies the **Al-Aqsa Mosque**. The place is therefore holy to Jews and Muslims, and there is repeated dispute over it.

gewusst: The slips of paper from the Western Wall are not thrown away but buried.
The largest stones of the wall are much heavier than a lorry.

teile.einleitung: “Religion is the opium of the people” is a famous sentence by Karl Marx. He wrote it in 1844 in the introduction to his critique of Hegel’s philosophy of right. The sentence is often quoted and interpreted in very different ways.
wichtigste: Karl Marx wrote the sentence in 1844.
Immediately before it, he calls religion the “sigh of the oppressed creature”.
In the 19th century opium was a common painkiller.
Marx meant: religion eases suffering, but does not change the causes.
Instead of “illusory happiness”, he demanded the real happiness of the people.
Heinrich Heine had already spoken of “spiritual opium” in 1840.
Lenin sharpened the phrase in 1905 to “opium for the people”.

abschnitte.text: **Karl Marx** was a German philosopher and economist. In 1844 he wrote the **Introduction to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right**. It begins with the statement that the **criticism of religion** is the prerequisite of all criticism. Marx thought that the criticism of religion in Germany was essentially finished. Now the criticism of heaven had to become criticism of **law and politics**.

Shortly before the famous sentence, Marx calls religion the **“sigh of the oppressed creature”** and the heart of a heartless world. For him, then, religion is an expression of real **misery** and at the same time a protest against it. **Opium** was at that time a common **painkiller**. Like it, religion eases suffering without removing the social **causes**. Marx therefore demanded, in place of **illusory happiness**, the **real happiness** of the people.

In his theory of society, Marx distinguishes between the **base** and the **superstructure**. To the base he counts the **economic conditions**, that is, how people work and who owns the factories and land. Religion, law, politics and morality make up the **superstructure**. According to Marx this is shaped by the base. So when the economy changes, people’s ideas change too.

The image was not entirely new. As early as **1840** the poet **Heinrich Heine**, in his writing on Ludwig Börne, spoke of sweet, sleep-inducing drops of **spiritual opium**. Marx knew Heine personally. In **1905** **Lenin**, in “Socialism and Religion”, wrote of religion as **“opium for the people”**. By this he meant that religion was deliberately given to workers as a sedative. This interpretation shaped the anti-religious policy in the **Soviet Union**.

To this day the sentence is often quoted in shortened form. Some see in it a pure **rejection** of religion. Others stress that Marx also took seriously the **suffering** of people, from which religion arises. Believers disagree with the view that religion is only consolation. For them faith gives support, hope and strength to act. The discussion shows how differently people can think about religion.

gewusst: In Marx’s original text it says “It is the opium of the people”, so “of” and not “for”.
Marx and Heine met in Paris in 1843.

teile.einleitung: A monastery is a place where nuns or monks live, pray and work together. There are monasteries in Christianity, but also in Buddhism and other religions. In Switzerland, monasteries have strongly shaped history, culture and landscape.
wichtigste: Women in a monastery are called nuns, men are called monks.
The saying “ora et labora” means “pray and work”.
The religious dress is called a habit, and many nuns also wear a veil.
Several times a day everyone meets for the Liturgy of the Hours.
The cloister is a walkway around an inner courtyard.
In the monastery garden grow medicinal herbs, vegetables and flowers.
Fahr Abbey on the Limmat is a convent of Benedictine nuns.

abschnitte.text: Whoever enters a monastery wants to devote their life entirely to God. The women are called **nuns**, the men **monks**. They belong to an **order**, that is, a community with its own rules. Well-known orders are the Benedictines, the Franciscans and the Capuchins. A monastery for men is led by an **abbot**, a convent for women by an **abbess** or prioress.

In the 6th century Saint **Benedict of Nursia** wrote a rule for monastic life. Its motto in Latin is **“ora et labora”**, that is, “pray and work”. The day is divided up exactly.
